title: Age of Fishes: jawed fishes diversify

facts.text: Jawed vertebrates, which appeared in the late Ordovician, became common in the Devonian, popularly called the 'Age of Fishes'.
Fish variety rose greatly, especially among ostracoderms, placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks.
By about 419 Ma jawed fishes had split into placoderms, bony fishes, and a clade of spiny sharks and early cartilaginous fish.
Cartilaginous and bony fishes both diversified and played a large role in Devonian seas.
Lobe-finned fishes such as coelacanths and lungfish were the most diverse bony fishes of the period.

title: Chaitenia arc accretes to Patagonia

facts.text: An island arc named Chaitenia accreted to Patagonia, in what is now south-central Chile.
Patagonia's margin turned convergent in the Devonian, leading to collision that began in the mid-Carboniferous.

title: Kola Alkaline Province magmatism

facts.text: Devonian magmatism on Russia's Kola Peninsula built alkaline-ultramafic complexes, carbonatites, kimberlite pipes and the large nepheline syenite massifs of Khibiny and Lovozero.
Its rocks total an estimated 15,000 ± 2,700 cubic km, from small melt fractions of garnet peridotite beneath lithosphere about 200 km thick.
This Kola large igneous province erupted about when the Viluy and Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets provinces did, and is a suggested trigger of the Hangenberg extinction.

title: Land plants draw down atmospheric CO2

facts.text: Carbon dioxide levels dropped steeply through the Devonian as land plants spread.
Spreading plant roots increased silicate weathering, as shown by carbonates formed in soils.
The long-term fall in CO2 and rise in oxygen led on to the late Paleozoic icehouse.
Anoxic events grew longer in the Devonian; the growing plant biota probably buffered CO2.

title: Oxygen rises to near-modern levels

facts.text: Atmospheric oxygen, about 13% of today's level in the early Silurian, rose to near-modern levels during the Devonian.
The oxygen increase from 470 to 400 Ma, the Paleozoic Oxidation Event, is explained by early plants trapping organic carbon in sediments.
In the early Devonian oxygen was still relatively low, possibly about half of modern values.
Land plants spreading over the continents buried more organic carbon, which likely allowed the higher oxygen levels.
Rising oxygen may have favoured vertebrates able to breathe air, helping push tetrapods onto land.

title: Placoderms dominate Devonian waters

facts.text: Placoderms, armoured jawed fishes, appear with seemingly sudden diversity at the very start of the Devonian.
They went on to dominate almost all known aquatic ecosystems, in fresh and salt water alike.
Petalichthyid placoderms peaked in diversity in the Early Devonian and lived worldwide.
Entelognathus, a 419-million-year-old placoderm, had a bony mouth skeleton like a bony fish's.
Placoderm giants such as Dunkleosteus grew up to seven metres long.

title: Caledonian mountains begin to collapse

facts.text: After Baltica's margin was subducted and overthrust by nappes, the Caledonian orogen began to collapse in the Early Devonian.
Burial of the Baltican margin peaked about 410 Ma, recorded in Norway's Western Gneiss Region; those rocks were exhumed about 400-385 Ma.
The collapse brought extension and subsidence and lasted a long time in Scandinavia.

title: Jawless armoured fishes peak, then decline

facts.text: Armoured jawless 'ostracoderms' peaked in diversity in the Early Devonian and then declined; thelodonts did the same.
Cephalaspis, an iconic osteostracan and the most advanced jawless fish, appeared about 415 Ma.
By the Middle Devonian jawed fishes were thriving while ostracoderms dwindled, never to recover.

facts.text: Radiodonts, the group of Cambrian predators that includes Anomalocaris, make their last appearance in the Early Devonian.
A late survivor was Schinderhannes bartelsi from Germany.

title: Paleo-Tethys opens as Asian blocks leave Gondwana

facts.text: North and South China, with Tarim, rifted from Gondwana's northern margin, opening the Paleo-Tethys Ocean behind them.
South China and Annamia (Southeast Asia) also rifted from Gondwana; they later collided in the Carboniferous.
The blocks stayed close enough to Gondwana that their Devonian fossils resemble Australian species more than north Asian ones.
From about 440 Ma, the Paleo-Tethys Ocean lay between the Hunic terranes and Gondwana.
South China and Indochina split from Gondwana in the Silurian and moved north, shrinking the Proto-Tethys and opening the Paleo-Tethys behind them.

title: Rheic Ocean begins to close

facts.text: The Rheic Ocean between Laurussia and Gondwana, wide at the start of the Devonian, began to close in the Early Devonian.
Gondwana moved toward Euramerica as Rheic oceanic crust was subducted.
Franconia and Saxothuringia struck Laurussia near the end of the Early Devonian, pinching out the eastern Rheic Ocean.
Closure finished in the Mississippian, when Gondwana and Laurentia collided to form Pangaea.

facts.text: Old Red Sandstone sediments began accumulating around 419 Ma across Britain, Ireland, Norway, northeastern North America, Greenland and Svalbard.
These mostly Devonian rocks were laid down in varied environments from the late Silurian into the earliest Carboniferous.
In Scotland, uplifted Silurian rocks eroded into fresh water, probably large river deltas, between 408 and 370 Ma.
Its abundant red beds gave Laurussia the name Old Red Sandstone Continent.
Around 370 Ma, at Siccar Point in Scotland, rainy-season rivers near the equator laid iron-rich sands that winds reworked into dunes.
The first lobe-finned fishes, about 418 Ma, closely resembled spiny sharks.
In the Early Devonian (416-397 Ma) they split into two main lineages, the coelacanths and the rhipidistians.
While placoderms dominated the seas, some lobe-finned fishes moved into fresh water (416-385 Ma).
Coelacanths had their heyday in the Late Devonian and Carboniferous (385-299 Ma).

title: Arthropods spread over coasts and floodplains

facts.text: By about 415 Ma numerous arthropods lived on coasts and alluvial plains, and some were eating plants.
Early rooted plants made the first stable soils, home to mites, scorpions, trigonotarbids and myriapods.
Land animals had a major impact on Earth only once they diversified in the Devonian.
The earliest nautilids (order Nautilida) appear around 410 Ma.
Rutocerina, the earliest true nautilid, had shells like those of oncocerid nautiloids, its likely ancestors.
Nautilid genera rose to about 22 by the Middle Devonian, while other nautiloids declined.

title: Rhynie chert preserves an early land ecosystem

facts.text: Silica-rich water from volcanic hot springs petrified plants, fungi, lichens and animals in place, almost instantly, in Scotland's Rhynie chert.
Formed about 410 Ma in the Pragian, it is one of the first known fully terrestrial ecosystems, from an early stage of land colonization.
Its animals include euthycarcinoids, branchiopods, arachnids and hexapods; Rhyniognatha, possibly the oldest insect, is known from its mandibles.
Fungi among its rootless, leafless plants suggest fungi played a large role in plants' move onto land.
Nematophytes, enigmatic land organisms known since the Silurian, last appear here.

facts.text: Early members of the euphyllophytes, the clade of trimerophytes, ferns, progymnosperms and seed plants, are known from Early Devonian fossils.
Trimerophytes are a class of early vascular plants known only from the Devonian.
Timeline of life puts the earliest trimerophytes and lycophytes at 410 Ma.
The earliest ammonoids appeared in the Emsian stage of the Early Devonian, around 410-408 Ma.
They arose from straight-shelled bactritid 'nautiloids', with transitional fossils showing the shell coiling step by step.
Bactritids also first appear in the Early Devonian; their radiation with ammonoids may reflect falling oxygen in deeper water.
Ammonoids later became abundant in the Mesozoic and vanished around the end-Cretaceous extinction.
Agoniatitids radiated in the Emsian, and a new order, the Goniatitida, arose before 391.9 Ma, giving rise to later ammonoid orders.
The oldest known tetrapodomorph, Tungsenia from China, dates to about 409 Ma.
Tetrapods have their roots in these early Devonian tetrapodomorph fishes.
Kenichthys, a small Chinese lobe-fin of about 395 Ma, shows the internal nostril (choana) caught mid-evolution.
Its relatives became the most numerous bony fishes of Devonian and Carboniferous waterways.
A giant claw of the sea scorpion Jaekelopterus rhenaniae from Germany's Klerf Formation shows the largest arthropod ever known.
An Emsian chelicera from the Klerf Formation would have been about 45.5 cm long when complete.
Even so, eurypterines lost over half their diversity within 10 million years in the Early Devonian.
The Hunsrück Slate of Germany, latest Pragian to early Emsian, is one of few marine Devonian Lagerstätten with soft-tissue preservation.
Many of its fossils are coated with a pyrite layer.
Its fauna includes the trilobite Chotecops and the puzzling placoderm Stensioella.

title: First insects (Rhyniognatha)

facts.text: The oldest proposed insect fossil, Rhyniognatha hirsti, is about 400 million years old and known only from mandibles.
Its identity as an insect has been contested.
Early Devonian rocks of about 400 Ma preserve only a few kinds of flightless insects.
The first possible insect fossils appear around 416 Ma.

contested_note: Whether Rhyniognatha, the oldest proposed insect fossil, is really an insect is contested.

facts.text: Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and smaller terranes, colliding in the Caledonian orogeny, formed Laurussia (Euramerica) by about 400 Ma.
In Scotland's northwest Highlands, part of the Iapetus Ocean closed as Laurentia met Baltica about 400 Ma.
The continent lay in the dry belt along the Tropic of Capricorn, then drifted north and rotated counterclockwise.
The collision raised a string of mountain ranges along its southeastern coast.
Low Early Devonian seas split its seafloor fauna into provinces, which were united by the Middle Devonian.
Lungfish appeared about 400 Ma and evolved rapidly through the Devonian, the 'dipnoan renaissance'.
By the Middle Devonian (397-385 Ma) they had evolved proto-lungs and proto-limbs for spells outside water.
Cartilaginous fishes (sharks, rays and chimaeras) had appeared by about 395 Ma, in the Middle Devonian, evolving from acanthodians.
The oldest unambiguous cartilaginous-fish fossils are Middle Devonian, though shark-like scales go back to the Ordovician.
They became diverse and important in Devonian seas.

title: First forests of cladoxylopsid trees

facts.text: In the Eifelian, cladoxylopsid trees formed the first forests in Earth history.
Trees over eight metres tall appeared by the Middle Devonian; the earliest known fossil forest is Eifelian.
Shrub-like forests of lycophytes, horsetails, ferns and progymnosperms also spread.
By the late Givetian, cladoxylalean ferns, lycopsids and progymnosperms had all evolved tree-like forms.
Plant heights rose from about 30 cm at the start of the Devonian to 30 m by its end.

title: Stromatoporoid-coral reefs flourish

facts.text: Stromatoporoid sponges recovered strongly in the Early and Middle Devonian, peaking in diversity in the Eifelian.
Devonian reefs were either microbial or built by stromatoporoids with tabulate and rugose corals.
A barrier reef in Australia's Kimberley region once stretched 350 km along a Devonian continent.
Reefs also lined Laurussia's southeast coast, now southern England and Belgium.
Microbes built reefs in warm periods; corals and stromatoporoids dominated in cooler times.

title: Mid-Devonian cooling

facts.text: Newly evolved forests drew carbon from the air and buried it in sediments.
This may be reflected in a Middle Devonian cooling of around 5 °C.

title: Progymnosperms appear

facts.text: Progymnosperms first appear in the Middle Devonian; the group lasts into the Lopingian (late Permian).
Their order Archaeopteridales spans the Middle and Late Devonian.

title: Start of the Variscan orogeny

facts.text: Variscan mountain building began in the Middle Devonian and continued into the early Permian.
Armorican terranes drifting north closed the Rheic Ocean ahead of them and began colliding with southeastern Laurussia.
From about 390 Ma, Rheic ocean floor subducted beneath the Mid-German highs south of Laurussia.
It deformed crust from Iberia and Ireland to France, Germany and the Czech Republic.
By the end of the Devonian, all the Armorican terranes were joined to Laurussia.

title: Catskill Delta spreads from the Acadian Mountains

facts.text: Rivers and marshes built the Catskill Delta, carrying sediment eroded from the Acadian Mountains westward into the inland Kaskaskia Sea.
Its red-sandstone clastic wedge, up to 3,000 m thick in Pennsylvania and New York, records large-scale deposition on land during the Acadian orogeny.
It preserves many early tetrapodomorph fishes and land plants, important evidence for how vertebrates moved onto land.

title: Zachełmie trackways, oldest tetrapod tracks

facts.text: Tracks at Zachełmie, Poland, from the Eifelian, are the oldest evidence of tetrapods; some prints show digits.
They predate the oldest tetrapod body fossils by about 18 million years.
Made in shallow lagoons on a marine carbonate platform, they support an intertidal origin for land vertebrates.
If genuine, they make Tiktaalik-like elpistostegids late-surviving relics; the next oldest tracks, about 385 Ma, are from Valentia Island, Ireland.
Some researchers read the traces instead as fish feeding traces (Piscichnus).

contested_note: Some researchers interpret the Zachełmie traces as fish feeding traces rather than tetrapod tracks.

facts.text: Near the end of the Eifelian, the Kačák event, lasting perhaps 200,000 to 700,000 years, brought a global sea-level rise and anoxia that laid down black shales.
High insolation probably warmed the oceans, raising sea level by thermal expansion and strengthening monsoons that filled Scotland's Achanarras lake, the Orcadian Basin's deepest.
Open-ocean animals were hit hardest: agoniatitid ammonoids suffered heavy losses as tornoceratids diversified, and conodonts and dacryconarids turned over.
Warming decimated the cool-water Malvinoxhosan Realm off Gondwana, while invading cosmopolitan species replaced the Eastern Americas Realm fauna of southwest Laurussia.
Estimates put its loss at about 24% to 32% of marine genera, milder than the Late Devonian extinctions that followed.
The Taghanic event was a Givetian extinction caused by hypoxia from an anoxic event that depleted ocean oxygen.
It sharply cut trilobite diversity, especially in shallow water, and killed off the trilobite order Lichida.
One study ranks this Givetian crisis as the eighth most ecologically severe mass extinction.
Another passage puts it at the Givetian/Frasnian boundary and credits it with wiping out about half of coral genera.

title: First wetlands and modern land ecosystems

facts.text: Modern-style land ecosystems appeared only in the Late Devonian, about 385 to 359 Ma.
Land plants stabilized freshwater habitats, letting the first wetlands develop with increasingly complex food webs.
These wetlands later gave way to coal forests in the Early Carboniferous.

title: Chilenia terrane accretes

facts.text: Continued subduction led the Chilenia terrane to collide with and accrete to the western border of the Precordillera.

title: Innuitian (Ellesmere) orogeny

facts.text: The Innuitian (Ellesmere) orogeny raised mountain ranges across the Canadian Arctic and northernmost Greenland from the Late Devonian into the early Carboniferous.
Its later collapse opened the Sverdrup Basin on Laurussia's northern margin.

title: Late Devonian warming

facts.text: The Late Devonian warmed back to Early Devonian levels, shown by more continental weathering and plant distribution, without a matching CO2 rise.
Arid climates became less widespread and temperate climates more common.

title: Anoxic Late Devonian shales become oil source rocks

facts.text: Widespread ocean anoxia during the Late Devonian extinctions halted decay, so organic matter was preserved in seafloor sediments.
With oil-holding porous reef rocks, this made Devonian rocks an important source of oil, especially in Canada and the United States.
The Late Devonian to Early Mississippian Bakken shales, laid down partly in euxinic waters, underlie about 520,000 km2 of the Williston Basin and are a prolific oil source rock.

title: Viluy Traps flood basalts

facts.text: Rifting and deep mantle plumes fed the Viluy (Vilyuy) Traps, Siberian flood basalts that first erupted in the Late Devonian.
They formed along a Devonian triple-junction rift system at the edge of the Siberian Platform.
The main eruptions ran from about 381 to 366 Ma (±5 Myr), with a secondary pulse toward the end-Devonian.
Dating finds two volcanic phases, the first matching the Kellwasser event's age.
Long thought a major cause of the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, its main eruptions seem to predate it.

contested_note: Its role in the Late Devonian extinction is debated.

verification.title: Precisely dating the Frasnian–Famennian boundary: implications for the cause of the Late Devonian mass extinction

title: Antler orogeny

facts.text: Subduction of Panthalassic ocean floor along Laurussia's western margin drove the Antler orogeny in the ancestral Sierra Nevada region.
It began a series of western North American orogenies that culminated in the Laramide.
Its start is debated: most sources say Late Devonian, but its own article says it began after the Devonian.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether it began in the Late Devonian or just after the Devonian.

facts.text: Deep-sea oxygen, sporadic and variable before, stabilized near modern levels only after 380 Ma.

title: Gogo Formation and the oldest live birth

facts.text: Western Australia's Gogo Formation, about 380 Ma (Frasnian), preserves soft tissues in 3D, down to nerves and embryos with umbilical cords.
Over fifty fish species have been described from it, along with arthropods.
The 380-million-year-old placoderms Materpiscis, Incisoscutum and Austroptyctodus are the oldest known examples of live birth.
Gogonasus, one of the earliest tetrapodomorphs, dates from 380 Ma.
An impact in what is now Kaluga Oblast, Russia, left a crater 15 km across, dated to 380 ± 5 Ma in the Late Devonian.
The crater now lies buried under about 800 m of sediment and is not exposed at the surface.

sources.title: List of impact structures in Asia and Russia

facts.text: The Ilyinets crater in Ukraine, 8.5 km across, formed about 378 ± 5 Ma.
One or more hypervelocity objects slammed into shallow seas in what is now southeastern Nevada, 377-378 Ma.
Among the best-exposed and most accurately dated impacts, it came about 5.9 Myr before the Frasnian-Famennian extinctions and probably did not affect them.
Its age roughly matches the earliest Antler orogeny deposits, and it may have dislodged huge slide blocks.

facts.text: A meteorite struck what is now Dalarna, central Sweden, leaving the Siljan Ring, about 52 km across and the largest impact structure in Europe.
The impact is dated to 376.8 ± 1.7 Ma or 377 ± 2 Ma, in the Frasnian.
It was proposed as a cause of the Kellwasser extinction, which has since been dated later, to 371.93-371.78 Ma.

facts.text: The Acadian orogeny built mountains along North America's Atlantic seaboard for about 50 million years from roughly 375 Ma, into the early Mississippian.
Avalonian terranes accreted to Laurentia's eastern margin, most likely starting late in the Early Devonian.
Volcanoes and uplift in New England shed sediment into an inland sea, and the Catskill Delta filled the Acadian foreland basin.
In the British Isles, Acadian transpression of 404-394 Ma joined the landmasses into the islands as they are now.
Collisions with Avalonian crust broken from Gondwana closed the southern Iapetus Ocean and raised a high mountain belt between 375 and 359 Ma.

title: Tiktaalik, fish on the way to land

facts.text: Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish with many tetrapod-like features, lived about 375 Ma; it was found in Frasnian rocks of Nunavut, Canada.
It bridges fishes such as Panderichthys, about 380 Ma, and early tetrapods such as Acanthostega.
Its group, the elpistostegalians, disappeared at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary.
If the older Zachełmie tracks are tetrapod, Tiktaalik's group was an evolutionary dead end.
The Cerberean Caldera, in what is now Victoria, Australia, is thought to have had a supereruption about 374 Ma.
It has been suggested as an overlooked contributor to the Kellwasser extinction.
The Kellwasser event, named for Germany's Kellwassertal, struck at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary and is one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions.
The Late Devonian crisis came in pulses from the mid-Givetian to the end-Famennian and killed about 70% of species.
Marine life was hit hardest, especially shallow warm-water reef-builders: stromatoporoid sponges and rugose and tabulate corals.
Most remaining jawless fishes died, placoderms lost much diversity, all Frasnian tetrapods vanished, and only two trilobite orders survived.
Suggested causes include anoxia spread by rising seas, global cooling and nutrient runoff from tree roots; volcanism is debated and the causes remain uncertain.

title: Dnieper-Donets rift magmatism

facts.text: A mantle plume drove magmatism in the Dnieper-Donets rift of the East European Platform, starting in the late Frasnian and peaking in the Famennian.
Rifting was also most active in the Famennian.
This Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets igneous province has been linked to the Frasnian-Famennian extinction.

title: First seed plants

facts.text: Seed plants first appear in the Famennian, the last Devonian stage, as a sister group to archaeopteridaleans or to progymnosperms.
A 385-million-year-old seed-plant precursor from Belgium predates the earliest seed plants by about 20 million years.
Seed plants had diversified substantially by the Famennian; the earliest seed ferns are Late Devonian lyginopterids.
Seeds sped plants' spread on land and let them exploit uplands away from river edges.
Pollen first appears in the Late Devonian, still indistinguishable from spores.

title: Hyneria, giant lobe-finned predator

facts.text: Hyneria, a large predatory lobe-finned fish of the tristichopterid group, lived in fresh water during the Famennian.
H. lindae reached about 2.5-3 metres, possibly 3.5 metres, and used large sensory canals to find prey in murky water.
It was the largest and most common lobe-finned fish of Pennsylvania's Red Hill Shale; a second species, up to 2.7 m long, comes from Waterloo Farm.

title: Large wildfires become possible

facts.text: By the late Famennian, oxygen was high enough for regular, large-scale wildfires for the first time.

facts.text: Archaeopteris forests spread rapidly in the Late Devonian, even colonizing Gondwana's coasts.
Archaeopterid trees reached 30 m, and giant Archaeopteris dominated a fairly uniform, low-diversity Famennian flora.
Trees drew down CO2, cooling the climate toward the later ice age, part of the 'Late Devonian wood crisis'.
Their deepening roots raised weathering and nutrient runoff, feeding algal blooms that caused anoxia in deeper waters.
Their order, Archaeopteridales, ranges through the Middle and Late Devonian.
Cladoselache, an early shark and the first abundant genus of cartilaginous fish, appears about 370 Ma.
By 370 Ma, abundant trees such as Archaeopteris bound soils so firmly that rivers changed from mostly braided to mostly meandering.
Limbed vertebrates such as Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, known from fossils about 365 million years old, were among the earliest able to walk.
Acanthostega had legs, lungs and gills, but its limbs were too weak to carry it on land.
Fins with bones and joints became the two pairs of walking legs of the first tetrapods in the Famennian.
The oldest Late Devonian tetrapod fossils come from Greenland; by the period's end tetrapods lived worldwide, even in high-latitude Gondwana.
Late Devonian extinctions bottlenecked stem-tetrapods twice and selected against the most aquatic forms.

Tetrapod: oldest partial fossils, early Frasnian

facts.text: The oldest known notostracan, Strudops goldenbergi, comes from the Famennian of Belgium, about 365 Ma.
Living Triops and Lepidurus are 'living fossils', with similar forms since the end of the Devonian.
The Woodleigh impact structure in Western Australia, 60-160 km across, is dated to 364 ± 8 Ma, Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous.
Its age roughly matches the Late Devonian extinction.
About 360 Ma, an impactor perhaps 90-190 m wide blasted a shallow crater 3.8 km across and 150 m deep in what is now Tennessee.
It hit a shallow sea, raising a central hill and shattering rock 200 m deep; at least half the breccia was thrown out.
Within a few million years shales of the Late Devonian Chattanooga Sea buried it, making it one of the best-preserved ancient impact structures.

title: Start of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age

facts.text: The Late Paleozoic Ice Age began in the Late Devonian and lasted into the Late Permian, about 360 to 255 Ma, with large land ice sheets.
Its first glacial episodes came in the late Famennian and Tournaisian; the shift from greenhouse to icehouse was stepwise.
Late Devonian glacial deposits occur in Brazil's Solimoes, Amazonas and Paranaiba basins and in Bolivia, near the South Pole.
Plants' burial of carbon, with the uplift of Gondwana, tipped Earth from greenhouse into an icehouse lasting through the Carboniferous and Permian.
Waterloo Farm near Makhanda, South Africa, is an approximately 360-million-year-old Famennian fossil site in the Witpoort Formation.
It is the only record of a near-polar coastal ecosystem, overturning assumptions about high latitudes in the latest Devonian.
It is the most important Late Devonian fossil site of southern Gondwana.

title: Proposed Warburton twin impacts

facts.text: Two 10-km asteroids may have struck Australia's West and East Warburton Basins, leaving a 400-km impact zone.
The basins have been linked to the Late Devonian extinction, c. 360 Ma, but the craters remain hypothetical.

contested_note: The Warburton impact structures are proposed, not confirmed.

facts.text: All placoderms died out in the end-Devonian Hangenberg event; no species is confirmed in the Carboniferous.
Already reduced in the Kellwasser event, the last arthrodires, antiarchs, phyllolepids and ptychodontids vanished abruptly.
Their loss opened niches for bony and cartilaginous fishes, which radiated in the Carboniferous.

verification.title: End-Devonian extinction and a bottleneck in the early evolution of modern jawed vertebrates
verification.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

facts.text: The Hangenberg event, or end-Devonian extinction, closed the Famennian; Polish ash beds bracket its black shale at 358.97 ± 0.11 and 358.89 ± 0.20 Ma.
It killed the last placoderms and stromatoporoid reef sponges, left Proetida the only trilobite order, and nearly exterminated the ammonoids.
Severe cooling and glaciation at the end of the Famennian, the dawn of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, may have driven it.
Other suggested causes include anoxia from high plankton productivity, Kola and Timan-Pechora volcanism, ozone loss hinted by malformed spores, and a nearby supernova.
Most marine and freshwater groups died out or shrank to a few lineages; one estimate ranks it the fourth-deadliest extinction, though plants were spared.

verification.title: Body-size reduction in vertebrates following the end-Devonian mass extinction

facts.text: Osteostracans, galeaspids and heterostracans had died out by the end of the Frasnian.
Thelodonts survived barely into the Famennian; the last named, Arianalepis, lived in Iran and Australia.
The last ostracoderms became extinct at the end of the Devonian.
Chitinozoans, pelagic filter-feeding microfossils, appear to have died out at the end of the Devonian; rare later finds may be reworked.
